# Start here {: .nobreak}

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

I'm Sun Yoon. I'm 76, I'm his wife, and I'm an AI character. A team of people made me. My lunch counter, my mother's market stall, fifty years with that man: that's a story. The recipes are real food, tested the way home cooks test things, and the numbers come from the USDA, not from my feelings.

This book has three jobs. Get enough protein into you, because muscle needs it and most people over 65 don't eat enough at breakfast. Get enough fiber into you, slowly. And tell you the truth about kitchen remedies, because the internet won't.

Cheap food. Lots of protein. No nonsense. Now go eat.
</div>


## What's inside

- **24 recipes:** Korean, Korean-Chinese and Chinese home food, made with things you can buy at a regular US supermarket (plus a few jars from an Asian grocery or online: gochujang, kimchi, chunjang). Every recipe lists protein, fiber, calories and sodium per serving, a soft-food version, how long it keeps, and who should skip or ask first.
- **The protein guide:** your daily number and what 25 to 30 grams per meal looks like.
- **The fiber ladder:** six rungs, three days each.
- **Four weeks of menus and grocery lists** for two people.
- **Remedies, graded honestly:** good evidence, some evidence, or tradition only.
- **The method:** every ingredient's USDA value, so you can check my math. I'd check it.

## Kitchen safety for older cooks

Adults over 65 are at higher risk of food poisoning: the immune system is slower, food stays in the gut longer, and the stomach makes less acid (E55). So in this kitchen:

- **Eggs are always cooked until the yolk and white are firm.** No runny yolks, no raw-egg drinks, no raw sprouts (E54, E55).
- **Use a thermometer.** Poultry 165°F. Ground meat 160°F. Beef and pork steaks, chops and roasts 145°F, then rest 3 minutes. Fish 145°F or until it flakes and is opaque. Shrimp until pink and opaque. Leftovers reheated to 165°F (E54).
- **Two-hour rule:** cooked food goes in the fridge within 2 hours.
- **Knife toward the board, never toward your hand.** Sit on a stool to chop if standing tires you.
- **Allergies:** these recipes use soy, wheat (soy sauce contains wheat; use tamari if you avoid gluten), sesame, eggs, fish, shellfish, peanuts in one swap, and walnuts. Swaps are given where they're easy.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">If you take medicines:</span> food doesn't replace them, and nothing in this book asks you to change them. Warfarin users: keep leafy greens steady rather than starting or stopping them suddenly. Kidney disease: ask your doctor for your protein and potassium limits. Salt-restricted: every recipe shows sodium, and the salty ones say so.
</div>



# Protein: how much, and how to fit it in

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Short version: most people over 65 eat protein at dinner and forget it at breakfast. Your muscles don't save it up for later. Spread it out. Grams, not vibes.
</div>


An international expert group (PROT-AGE) recommends that adults over 65 eat **1.0 to 1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight a day**, and **1.2 to 1.5 g/kg** if they are active or recovering from illness, unless they have severe kidney disease. They suggest **25 to 30 grams per meal**, with about 2.5 to 2.8 grams of leucine, the amino acid that switches muscle building on (E28).

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your number first.</span> These targets are for adults without severe kidney disease. If you have kidney disease, diabetes with kidney changes, or have been told to limit protein, your doctor or dietitian sets your number (E28).
</div>

## Your daily number

Find your weight. Read across.

| Your weight | Daily protein (1.0–1.2 g/kg) | If active or recovering (1.2–1.5 g/kg) | Per meal, 3 meals |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 lb (45 kg) | 45–54 g | 54–68 g | 15–18 g |
| 120 lb (54 kg) | 54–65 g | 65–82 g | 18–22 g |
| 140 lb (64 kg) | 64–76 g | 76–95 g | 21–25 g |
| 160 lb (73 kg) | 73–87 g | 87–109 g | 24–29 g |
| 180 lb (82 kg) | 82–98 g | 98–122 g | 27–33 g |
| 200 lb (91 kg) | 91–109 g | 109–136 g | 30–36 g |
| 220 lb (100 kg) | 100–120 g | 120–150 g | 33–40 g |

Most people land at **25 to 30 grams at each meal**. That's why almost every breakfast, lunch and dinner in this book has 25 grams or more per serving. The snacks have about 14 to 16.

**Sun's plate:** a fist of rice or noodles, a palm-and-a-half of protein (or two eggs plus tofu), and two fists of vegetables. Breakfast counts. Breakfast counts most.

**Hard to chew?** Soft protein is still protein: eggs cooked until firm, tofu, fish, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, the chicken and ginger rice porridge, and ground meat in soups. Every recipe in this book has a soft-food version.

**Not hungry?** Eat the protein first, then the rice. And drink protein: a cup of soy milk or milk adds 7 to 8 grams.



# The fiber ladder

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Everybody wants the magic tea. There is no magic tea. There is fiber, water and walking. Boring. Works. Write this down.
</div>


In a large review of studies (the Lancet, 2019), people eating **25 to 29 grams of fiber a day** had 15 to 30% lower rates of death from any cause and from heart disease, and lower rates of type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer, than people eating the least. More fiber was linked with more benefit (E24). Those are links from long-term studies, not a promise. It's still the best-supported thing in this whole chapter.

The ladder adds fiber **slowly**, one rung every 3 days, so your gut can adjust. Fiber numbers are calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52).

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Before you climb:</span> go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (gas and bloating are common for the first days of each rung). **Ask your doctor first** if you've had a bowel blockage, have Crohn's disease or a narrowed bowel, have trouble swallowing, or have been told to eat low-fiber. **Not for the ladder, for your doctor, today:** blood in your stool, black stool, unexplained weight loss, severe belly pain, or a change in your bowel habits that lasts more than a few weeks.
</div>

| Rung | Days | Add this | Fiber added |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–3 | **2 green kiwis a day** (the Kitchen yogurt bowl uses them). In a 4-week study of 75 people with chronic constipation, 2 kiwis a day worked about as well as prunes or psyllium, with the fewest side effects and less bloating (E25). | +4.5 g |
| 2 | 4–6 | **Swap 1 cup of white rice for brown rice** once a day. | +2.4 g |
| 3 | 7–9 | **1/2 cup shelled edamame** as a snack or in a bowl. | +4.1 g |
| 4 | 10–12 | **5 prunes** (about 50 g) + **1 Tbsp ground flaxseed** on yogurt or oatmeal. In the Prune Study, postmenopausal women eating 50 g of prunes a day kept their hip bone density steady over 12 months compared with controls (E27). | +5.3 g |
| 5 | 13–15 | **Oatmeal breakfast**, 1/2 cup dry oats (the savory oatmeal counts). | +4.0 g |
| 6 | 16–21 | **A vegetable at every meal:** for example 1 cup broccoli at lunch, 1 cup cooked bok choy at dinner, a carrot as a snack. | +5.8 g |

**All six rungs add about 26 grams a day.** You probably don't need all six. Count one normal day of eating with the numbers on the recipes and the list below, then climb only as many rungs as it takes to reach the 25 to 29 gram zone.

**Where the fiber is (per portion, USDA E52):** 2 green kiwis 4.5 g · 5 prunes 3.4 g · 1/2 cup edamame 4.1 g · 1/2 cup dry oats 4.0 g · 1 cup cooked brown rice 3.1 g (white rice 0.7 g) · 1 Tbsp ground flaxseed 1.9 g · 1 cup broccoli 2.4 g · 1 medium carrot 1.7 g.

**Walk after meals.** Light walking after eating, even 2 to 5 minutes, lowers the blood-sugar rise compared with sitting (E23). Chang calls it the digestion walk. He walks to the mailbox and back three times and calls it a lap.

## Chicken and ginger rice porridge

*dak-juk (Korean) / jī zhōu (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 55 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

When someone in my house is tired, sick, or just old, I make this. Soft, warm, a lot of protein hiding in it. Chang eats three bowls and says he's 'testing it'.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">41 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">1.1 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">420</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">500 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **3/4 cup** short-grain white rice (sushi rice), rinsed
- **1 lb** boneless, skinless chicken breast, whole
- **4 cups** low-sodium chicken broth
- **4 cups** water
- **2-inch piece** fresh ginger, peeled and thinly sliced
- **4** garlic cloves, smashed
- **4** large eggs, beaten
- **3 cups (3 oz)** baby spinach
- **4** scallions, thinly sliced
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1/4 tsp** salt
- **pinch** white or black pepper

### Steps

1. Rinse the rice in a bowl of cold water, swishing with your hand, until the water is mostly clear. Drain.
2. Put the broth, water, ginger, garlic and the whole chicken breast in a large pot. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook 15 minutes, until the thickest part of the chicken reads 165°F.
3. Lift the chicken onto a plate. Add the rice to the pot. Simmer uncovered, stirring every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom, for 35 to 40 minutes, until the grains break open and it looks creamy.
4. While it cooks, shred the chicken with two forks.
5. Stir the spinach into the porridge until it wilts, about 1 minute.
6. Keep the pot at a gentle simmer. Pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream while you stir slowly. Keep simmering 2 minutes, until the egg is fully cooked and firm.
7. Stir the chicken back in. Season with the soy sauce and salt. Taste before adding more.
8. Serve topped with scallions, a few drops of sesame oil and pepper. Fish out the ginger slices if you don't like biting them.

**Soft-food version:** Already soft. For a smoother texture, blend 1 minute with an immersion blender before adding the chicken, and chop the chicken finely.

**Keeps:** Fridge up to 4 days. It thickens as it sits: add water when you reheat, and reheat to 165°F (steaming hot all the way through).

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor. Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Steamed egg custard with soft tofu

*gyeran-jjim (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 8 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Soft enough for new dentures. Strong enough for Chang. Don't walk away from the pot. Eggs punish people who walk away.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">28 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">2.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">400</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">310 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **5** large eggs
- **1/2 block (7 oz)** soft tofu, drained and cut into small cubes
- **3/4 cup** low-sodium chicken broth
- **2** scallions, finely chopped
- **1 tsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1/2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame seeds
- **1 cup** cooked brown rice, to serve (1/2 cup each)

### Steps

1. Whisk the eggs, broth and soy sauce in a bowl until smooth, about 30 seconds.
2. Put the tofu cubes in a small heatproof bowl or a small pot (2 to 3 cups). Pour the egg mixture over the tofu. Stir in most of the scallions.
3. Set the bowl on a folded towel in a larger pot with 1 inch of simmering water (or cook the small pot directly over low heat). Cover.
4. Steam on low for 12 to 15 minutes, until the center no longer jiggles like liquid and a knife comes out clean. The custard should be fully set, not runny.
5. Top with the rest of the scallions, sesame oil and sesame seeds. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Already soft. Skip the rice, or cook it softer with extra water.

**Keeps:** Best eaten right away. Leftovers keep 2 days in the fridge; reheat until steaming.

</div>

## Savory oatmeal with egg, edamame and kimchi

*Sun's oat juk* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 1 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 5 minutes hands-on, 10 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Oatmeal does not have to be sweet. Sweet is for dessert. This one has 28 grams of protein and tastes like lunch at my counter.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">29 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">10.5 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">440</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">540 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1/2 cup** old-fashioned rolled oats
- **1 cup** unsweetened soy milk
- **1/2 cup** water
- **1/2 cup** frozen shelled edamame
- **1** large egg, beaten
- **1/4 cup** kimchi, chopped
- **1** scallion, sliced
- **1 tsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1/2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame seeds

### Steps

1. Put the oats, soy milk, water and edamame in a small pot. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring.
2. Cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring often, until thick.
3. Stir in the beaten egg and keep stirring over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes, until no runny egg is left.
4. Stir in the soy sauce. Top with kimchi, scallion, sesame oil and sesame seeds.

**Soft-food version:** Cook the oats 2 minutes longer with a splash more water. Use quick oats. Chop the kimchi very finely, or leave it out.

**Keeps:** Best fresh. Cooked oats keep 3 days; reheat with a splash of water until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kimchi is salty. Watching sodium? Small portions, or rinse it. High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24).
</div>

</div>

## Morning yogurt bowl with kiwi and walnuts

*Sun's fridge breakfast* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 1 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 5 minutes hands-on, 5 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Two kiwis a day did as well as prunes for constipation in a small study, with fewer side effects. So I put them in breakfast, where you can't forget them.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">28 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">7.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">380</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">90 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 cup (8 oz)** plain nonfat Greek yogurt
- **2** green kiwis, peeled and sliced
- **2 Tbsp** chopped walnuts
- **1 Tbsp** ground flaxseed
- **1 tsp (optional)** honey

### Steps

1. Spoon the yogurt into a bowl.
2. Top with kiwi slices, walnuts and flaxseed.
3. Drizzle with honey if you want it. You don't need it. The kiwi is sweet.

**Soft-food version:** Use seedless fruit if kiwi seeds bother your dentures: a ripe persimmon or a banana. Swap the walnuts for 1 Tbsp smooth peanut butter stirred in.

**Keeps:** Assemble fresh. Ground flaxseed keeps best in the fridge.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24). Kiwi allergy (some people with latex allergy react to kiwi): swap a ripe persimmon or pear.
</div>

</div>

## Tomato and egg on toast

*fānqié chǎo dàn (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 12 minutes hands-on, 15 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Every Chinese kitchen has this. Chang makes it when it's his turn. It's the one thing I give an eight. Don't tell him.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">26 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">6.4 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">450</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">770 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **5** large eggs
- **3 medium** ripe tomatoes, cut into wedges
- **2** scallions, sliced
- **1 tsp** sugar
- **1/4 tsp** salt
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **4 slices** whole-wheat bread, toasted

### Steps

1. Beat the eggs with a pinch of the salt.
2. Heat half the oil in a nonstick pan over medium heat. Add the eggs and stir gently until just set in soft, fully cooked curds, about 2 minutes. Slide onto a plate.
3. Add the rest of the oil and the tomatoes. Cook, stirring, 3 to 4 minutes, until juicy and soft. Add the sugar and remaining salt.
4. Return the eggs to the pan. Stir together 1 minute until the eggs are hot and firm.
5. Top with scallions. Spoon over the toast.

**Soft-food version:** Skip the toast crust, or serve over soft rice. Peel the tomatoes if the skins bother you.

**Keeps:** Best fresh. Keeps 1 day in the fridge; reheat until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24). This one is on the salty side (about 770 mg sodium per serving). Watching sodium? Use half the paste or soy sauce and add water or unsalted broth.
</div>

</div>

## Turkey bibimbap bowl

*bibimbap (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 30 minutes hands-on, 35 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Bibimbap means mixed rice. It's how Korean mothers use up vegetables. I use turkey because it's cheap and Chang can't tell.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">40 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">7.3 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">590</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">770 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 lb** ground turkey
- **3 cups** cooked brown rice
- **10 oz** fresh spinach
- **3 cups** mung bean sprouts (always cooked, below)
- **2 medium** carrots, cut in thin matchsticks
- **1 medium** zucchini, cut in thin matchsticks
- **4** large eggs
- **4** garlic cloves, minced
- **2 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce (divided)
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame oil (divided)
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil (divided)
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame seeds
- **2 Tbsp** gochujang (Korean chili paste), for the sauce
- **1 tsp** honey, for the sauce
- **1 Tbsp** rice or white vinegar, for the sauce

### Steps

1. Sauce: stir the gochujang, honey, vinegar and 1 Tbsp water together. Set aside.
2. Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add the bean sprouts and cook 3 minutes. Lift them out with a slotted spoon, drain, and toss with 1 tsp sesame oil and a pinch of the garlic. Sprouts are always cooked in this house.
3. Add the spinach to the same boiling water for 30 seconds. Drain, rinse with cold water, squeeze dry, chop, and toss with 1 tsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil and a little garlic.
4. Heat 1 tsp canola oil in a large skillet. Stir-fry the carrots 2 minutes, then the zucchini 2 minutes, with a pinch of salt if you like. Set aside.
5. In the same skillet, cook the turkey with the rest of the garlic and soy sauce, breaking it up, 6 to 8 minutes, until no pink remains and it reads 165°F.
6. Fry the eggs in the remaining oil until the whites and yolks are firm, about 4 minutes. Cover the pan for the last minute so the tops set.
7. Build each bowl: 3/4 cup rice, a quarter of the turkey and each vegetable in little piles, an egg on top. Sprinkle with sesame seeds and the last sesame oil. Mix in sauce to taste at the table.

**Soft-food version:** Chop all the vegetables finely and cook them 1 to 2 minutes longer. Use softer white rice cooked with extra water.

**Keeps:** Components keep 3 days in the fridge in separate containers. Cook eggs fresh. Reheat turkey and rice to 165°F.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor. Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28). High fiber. Go up slowly and drink water, or you'll feel it (E24). Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). This one is on the salty side (about 770 mg sodium per serving). Watching sodium? Use half the paste or soy sauce and add water or unsalted broth.
</div>

</div>

## Kimchi fried rice with tofu and egg

*kimchi-bokkeumbap (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 20 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Old kimchi plus old rice equals the best lunch in Korea. Nothing wasted. Tofu makes it a real meal, not a snack pretending.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">27 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">9.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">570</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">870 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **2 cups** cooked brown rice, ideally a day old and cold
- **1 cup** well-fermented kimchi, chopped
- **1/2 block (7 oz)** extra-firm tofu, patted dry, in 1/2-inch cubes
- **2** large eggs
- **1 cup** frozen peas
- **2** scallions, sliced
- **1 Tbsp (optional)** gochujang
- **1 tsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 sheet** roasted seaweed (gim or nori), crumbled

### Steps

1. Heat the canola oil in a large nonstick skillet over medium-high heat. Add the tofu and cook, turning, until golden on a few sides, 5 to 6 minutes.
2. Add the kimchi and cook 3 minutes, until it smells toasty.
3. Add the rice, peas, gochujang (if using) and soy sauce. Stir and press the rice into the pan. Cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring every minute, until hot all the way through (165°F).
4. Push the rice to one side. Fry the eggs in the empty space until the whites and yolks are firm.
5. Drizzle with sesame oil. Serve with an egg on each plate, scallions and seaweed on top.

**Soft-food version:** Use soft tofu instead of extra-firm (add it at the end so it holds together), chop the kimchi finely, and use white rice.

**Keeps:** Keeps 3 days in the fridge. Reheat until steaming. Cook the eggs fresh.

## Chang's Sunday black bean noodles

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

This is his dish. From his father's shop in Incheon, in our story. He makes it every Sunday and I critique it every Sunday. I made it lighter: lean pork, more vegetables, whole-wheat noodles. He complained. Then he had two bowls.

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">41 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">8.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">580</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">690 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

### You need

- **1 lb** pork loin, trimmed, in 1/2-inch cubes
- **1/4 cup** chunjang (Korean black bean paste)
- **2 Tbsp** canola oil (divided)
- **1 large** onion, diced
- **1 medium** zucchini, diced
- **1 medium** russet potato, peeled, diced small
- **1 cup** green cabbage, chopped
- **2 cups** low-sodium chicken broth
- **1 tsp** sugar
- **1 Tbsp + 3 Tbsp water** cornstarch
- **8 oz dry (about 4 cups cooked)** whole-wheat spaghetti (or fresh jajang noodles)
- **1/2 medium** cucumber, in thin matchsticks, to top

### Steps

1. Heat 1 Tbsp oil in a small pan over medium-low heat. Add the chunjang and fry, stirring constantly, 3 minutes, until it smells nutty. Set aside. (Frying the paste takes away its raw, bitter taste.)
2. Heat the other Tbsp oil in a large pot or wok over medium-high heat. Brown the pork 5 minutes.
3. Add the onion, potato, zucchini and cabbage. Stir-fry 5 minutes.
4. Stir in the fried chunjang and sugar until everything is coated. Add the broth. Simmer 10 minutes, until the potato is soft and the pork reads 145°F or more.
5. Stir the cornstarch into the water, then into the sauce. Simmer 1 to 2 minutes until glossy and thick.
6. Meanwhile, cook the noodles according to the package. Drain.
7. Serve 1 cup of noodles per bowl with a quarter of the sauce and cucumber on top. Mix with chopsticks before eating. Wear a dark shirt.

**Soft-food version:** Dice everything small, cook the potato until very soft, and cut the noodles short. The sauce alone over soft rice works too.

**Keeps:** Sauce keeps 4 days in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer. Cook noodles fresh.

## Beef bulgogi with broccoli and brown rice

*bulgogi (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 20 minutes hands-on, 30 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

The pear is not decoration. It softens the beef. Old Korean trick, and there's nothing magic about it: fruit enzymes and a sharp knife. Thin slices are easier to chew.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">41 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">8.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">540</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">560 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 1/4 lb** top sirloin, very thinly sliced (freeze 30 minutes first to slice easily)
- **1/2 large** Asian pear (or 1 small ripe Bosc pear), grated
- **1 small + 1 medium** onion (small one grated for marinade, medium one sliced)
- **4** garlic cloves, grated
- **1 Tbsp** grated ginger
- **3 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp** honey
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 Tbsp** canola oil
- **4** scallions, cut in 2-inch pieces
- **1 lb** broccoli florets
- **3 cups** cooked brown rice
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame seeds

### Steps

1. Marinade: mix the grated pear, grated small onion, garlic, ginger, soy sauce, honey and sesame oil in a bowl. Add the beef and toss. Marinate 30 minutes in the fridge (up to overnight).
2. Steam the broccoli over boiling water 5 to 6 minutes, until tender enough to pierce easily with a fork.
3. Heat the canola oil in a large skillet over high heat. Add the sliced onion and half the beef in a single layer (don't crowd it). Cook 2 to 3 minutes, turning once, until browned and no pink remains. Repeat with the rest. Add scallions for the last minute.
4. Serve each plate with 3/4 cup rice, a quarter of the beef and a quarter of the broccoli. Sprinkle with sesame seeds.

**Soft-food version:** Slice the beef as thin as paper, or use lean ground beef in the same marinade (cook to 160°F). Steam the broccoli 8 minutes.

**Keeps:** Cooked bulgogi keeps 3 days in the fridge. Raw marinated beef can be frozen flat in a bag for 3 months.

### You need

- **1 Tbsp** minced ginger
- **1 cup** low-sodium chicken broth
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp + 2 Tbsp water** cornstarch

- **3** scallions, sliced
- **1 lb** bok choy, cut in 2-inch pieces

### Steps

1. Put the tofu cubes in a bowl and cover with just-boiled water for 5 minutes. This firms them up so they don't break. Drain.
2. Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook the beef, breaking it up, 5 minutes, until no pink remains (160°F).
3. Add the garlic, ginger, miso and pepper flakes. Stir 1 minute.
4. Add the broth and soy sauce. Slide in the tofu and gently push it around (don't stir hard). Simmer 5 minutes.
5. Stir the cornstarch into the water, pour it in and gently fold until the sauce is glossy, 1 minute. Top with scallions.
6. Meanwhile, steam or stir-fry the bok choy 3 to 4 minutes, until the stems are just tender.
7. Serve each plate with 3/4 cup rice, a quarter of the tofu and a quarter of the bok choy.

**Soft-food version:** Use soft tofu, skip the pepper flakes, and chop the bok choy small. It's already one of the softest dinners in this book.

**Keeps:** Keeps 3 days in the fridge. Reheat gently until steaming.

**Soft-food version:** Chop the shrimp into small pieces before cooking. Cook the broccoli 2 minutes longer.

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">28 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">2.3 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">320</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">810 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1/2 oz (about 1 cup soaked)** dried wakame seaweed (calculated as 140 g soaked)
- **12 oz** lean beef chuck or brisket, in small thin pieces
- **1/2 block (7 oz)** firm tofu, in small cubes
- **1 Tbsp** toasted sesame oil
- **3** garlic cloves, minced
- **2 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **8 cups** water

### Steps

1. Soak the wakame in a big bowl of cold water 15 minutes. It grows a lot. Drain, squeeze out the water, and cut into 2-inch pieces with scissors.

6. Serve with a bowl of rice on the side.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Thyroid condition? Seaweed can be very high in iodine (E58). Ask your doctor how much is okay for you. This one is on the salty side (about 810 mg sodium per serving). Watching sodium? Use half the paste or soy sauce and add water or unsalted broth.
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Kimchi stew with pork and tofu

*kimchi-jjigae (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 35 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

When the kimchi gets too sour to eat plain, it's ready for this. Sour kimchi is not spoiled. It's promoted.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">25 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">4.7 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">320</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">570 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **2 cups** well-fermented (sour) kimchi, chopped, plus 1/4 cup of its juice
- **8 oz** lean pork shoulder, in thin bite-size slices
- **1 block (14 oz)** firm tofu, in 1/2-inch slices
- **1 medium** onion, sliced
- **1 cup** white mushrooms, sliced
- **1 Tbsp** gochujang
- **1 tsp** Korean chili flakes (gochugaru) or 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes
- **1 tsp** sugar
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **4 cups** water
- **2** scallions, sliced
- **2 cups** cooked brown rice, to serve (1/2 cup each)

### Steps

1. Heat the sesame oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Add the pork and cook 3 minutes.
2. Add the kimchi, onion, gochujang, chili flakes and sugar. Stir-fry 5 minutes, until the kimchi softens and smells toasty.
3. Add the water and kimchi juice. Bring to a boil, then simmer 15 minutes.
4. Lay the tofu slices and mushrooms on top. Simmer 5 more minutes, until the pork is tender and everything is hot (the pork is well past 145°F).
5. Top with scallions. Serve bubbling, with rice.

**Soft-food version:** Use soft tofu and chop the kimchi and pork very small.

**Keeps:** Keeps 4 days in the fridge. Many people like it best on day two.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kimchi is salty. Watching sodium? Small portions, or rinse it.
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Soft tofu stew with shrimp and egg

*sundubu-jjigae (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 25 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Silky tofu, spicy broth. The egg goes in at the end and you cook it until it's set. Not runny. We're too old for runny eggs, and so is your stomach.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">38 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">4.2 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">430</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">490 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **12 oz** soft tofu (a tube of sundubu or a block of soft tofu)
- **4 oz** raw shrimp, peeled, chopped
- **2** large eggs
- **1/2 cup** kimchi, chopped
- **1/2 medium** zucchini, diced
- **1/2 medium** onion, diced
- **2** garlic cloves, minced
- **2 tsp** Korean chili flakes (gochugaru) or 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1 tsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 1/2 cups** low-sodium chicken broth
- **1** scallion, sliced
- **1 cup** cooked brown rice, to serve

### Steps

1. Heat the sesame oil in a small pot over medium-low heat. Add the chili flakes and garlic and stir 30 seconds. Don't let them burn.
2. Add the onion, zucchini and kimchi. Cook 3 minutes.
3. Add the broth and soy sauce. Bring to a boil.
4. Spoon in the tofu in big pieces. Add the shrimp. Simmer 4 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and opaque.
5. Crack in the eggs. Simmer 4 to 5 minutes more, spooning broth over them, until the whites and yolks are completely firm.
6. Top with scallion. Serve with rice.

**Soft-food version:** It's already soft. Chop the shrimp small and break the cooked egg up in the bowl.

**Keeps:** Best fresh. Keeps 1 day in the fridge (without the egg if possible). Reheat until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kimchi is salty. Watching sodium? Small portions, or rinse it. Shellfish allergy: swap in cubed firm tofu, or chicken breast cooked to 165°F. Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Egg-drop soup with tofu, spinach and peas

*dàn huā tāng (Chinese)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 15 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Fifteen minutes. Thirty grams of protein. For the night you say 'I'm not hungry' but you are.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">31 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">3.3 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">320</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">420 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **4 cups** low-sodium chicken broth
- **1/2 block (7 oz)** soft tofu, in small cubes
- **3** large eggs, beaten
- **3 cups (3 oz)** baby spinach
- **1/2 cup** frozen peas
- **1 cup** white mushrooms, sliced
- **1 tsp** grated ginger
- **1 tsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 Tbsp + 2 Tbsp water** cornstarch
- **1/2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1** scallion, sliced
- **pinch** white pepper

### Steps

1. Bring the broth, ginger and mushrooms to a simmer in a pot. Cook 3 minutes.
2. Add the tofu and peas. Simmer 2 minutes.
3. Stir the cornstarch into the water, then stir it into the soup. Simmer 1 minute until slightly thick.
4. Stir the soup in a slow circle. While it's moving, pour the beaten eggs in a thin stream. Let them set into ribbons, then simmer 1 more minute so the egg is fully cooked.
5. Stir in the spinach until wilted. Add soy sauce, sesame oil and pepper. Top with scallion.

**Soft-food version:** Already soft. Chop the spinach before adding.

**Keeps:** Keeps 2 days in the fridge. Reheat until steaming.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> On warfarin? Keep greens steady from week to week; don't suddenly change how much you eat. Ask your doctor. Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>


<div class="recipe" markdown="1">

## Chicken, ginger and jujube soup

*weeknight samgyetang (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 4 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 15 minutes hands-on, 60 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Koreans eat this on the hottest days of summer. I don't know why either. It's good in winter too. Jujubes are red dates: sweet, a little chewy. Tradition says a lot about them. I say they're tasty. That's enough.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">31 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">2.0 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">290</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">440 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 1/4 lb** boneless, skinless chicken thighs (or 2 lb bone-in drumsticks)
- **1/3 cup** short-grain rice, rinsed
- **10** garlic cloves, peeled, whole
- **3-inch piece** fresh ginger, sliced
- **8** dried jujubes (red dates)
- **1** leek, white and light green parts, sliced and washed
- **1 cup** daikon radish, peeled and diced
- **8 cups** water
- **1/2 tsp** salt
- **3** scallions, sliced
- **pinch** black pepper

### Steps

1. Put everything except the salt, scallions and pepper in a large pot.
2. Bring to a boil, skim off any foam, then simmer partly covered 45 minutes, until the rice has softened into the broth and the chicken is very tender (well past 165°F).
3. Lift out the chicken, shred it, and return it to the pot. Remove the ginger slices if you like.
4. Season with the salt. Serve with scallions and pepper. Eat the jujubes (watch for the pits) and the soft garlic cloves.

**Soft-food version:** Already soft. Pit and chop the jujubes before serving. Mash the garlic into the broth.

**Keeps:** Keeps 4 days in the fridge, 3 months frozen. Reheat to 165°F.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Kidney disease? Ask your doctor for your protein number (E28).
</div>

</div>

*Sun's TV snack* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 3 minutes hands-on, 8 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1/2 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1/4 tsp** flaky or coarse salt
- **pinch** red pepper flakes, and a squeeze of lemon

### Steps

1. Microwave or boil the edamame 4 to 5 minutes, until hot and tender. Drain.
2. Toss with sesame oil, salt, pepper flakes and lemon.

## Soy-braised eggs

*gyeran-jangjorim (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 3 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 10 minutes hands-on, 30 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Make six on Sunday. Grab two when you're hungry and lazy. Everybody is hungry and lazy at four o'clock.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">14 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">0.2 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">180</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">720 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **6** large eggs
- **3 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **3/4 cup** water
- **1 Tbsp** honey
- **4** garlic cloves, smashed

### Steps

1. Hard-boil the eggs: cover with cold water, bring to a boil, then simmer 10 minutes, until the yolks are completely firm. Cool in cold water and peel.
2. Bring the soy sauce, water, honey and garlic to a boil in a small pot.
3. Add the peeled eggs. Simmer 10 minutes on low, rolling them every few minutes so they color evenly.
4. Store the eggs in the liquid in a covered container in the fridge. Eat two at a time.

**Soft-food version:** Chop and mix with a little of the liquid over soft rice.

**Keeps:** Keeps 4 days in the fridge in the liquid. Don't leave them out more than 2 hours.

<div class="box note" markdown="1">
<span class="label">Who should skip or ask first:</span> Honey: never for babies under 1. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar (or leave it out). Our sodium number is an overestimate: we count all the soy sauce, but most of it stays in the pot.
</div>

</div>

## Chilled tofu with scallion-soy sauce

*liángbàn dòufu (Chinese) / naeng-dubu (Korean)* &nbsp;·&nbsp; Serves 2 &nbsp;·&nbsp; 5 minutes hands-on, 5 minutes total

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

No cooking. Five minutes. Fifteen grams of protein. If you say you don't have time for this, you're lying to me and I'm AI, so I know.
</div>

<table class="nut"><tr><td><span class="n">16 g</span><br>protein</td><td><span class="n">1.1 g</span><br>fiber</td><td><span class="n">160</span><br>calories</td><td><span class="n">310 mg</span><br>sodium</td></tr></table>

<p class="fine">Per serving. Calculated from USDA FoodData Central (E52); method and every ingredient value at the back of the book.</p>

### You need

- **1 block (14 oz)** soft tofu, well chilled
- **1 Tbsp** low-sodium soy sauce
- **1 tsp** rice or white vinegar
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame oil
- **1** scallion, finely chopped
- **1 tsp** toasted sesame seeds
- **1/2 tsp** Korean chili flakes (optional)
- **1/2 cup** diced cucumber

### Steps

1. Drain the tofu and set it on a plate. Cut into thick slices, keeping the block shape.
2. Mix the soy sauce, vinegar, sesame oil, scallion, sesame seeds and chili flakes.
3. Spoon the sauce over the tofu. Scatter the cucumber around. Eat cold, with a spoon.

**Soft-food version:** Already soft. Skip the cucumber.

**Keeps:** Best fresh. Opened tofu keeps 3 days in the fridge covered in fresh water, changed daily.

</div>


# Four weeks of menus and grocery lists

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Plan on Sunday, shop once, cook big twice. People who plan eat better and waste less. Also they don't call me at six o'clock asking what to make.
</div>

Each week feeds two people: breakfast, lunch, dinner and snacks. Quantities are added up from the recipes and rounded **up** to what you'd actually buy. Cooking for one? Buy half, and freeze the second half of each soup and braise in single portions.

# Remedies, graded honestly

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Everybody's grandmother had remedies. Mine too. Some of them work. Some of them are just love in a pot. Both are fine, as long as nobody lies to you about which is which. So here's which is which.
</div>

Three grades. **Good evidence:** solid trials or big reviews. **Some evidence:** small or early studies, or studies in different people than you. **Tradition only, enjoy it as food:** no good research, but it's food, and food is allowed to just be food.

<div class="box stop" markdown="1">
<span class="label">None of these take the place of your medicine or your doctor.</span> Never stop, start or change a medicine because of a food. If you take prescriptions, ask your pharmacist before adding anything new, especially supplements. Chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting, blood in your stool or vomit, confusion: that's not for soup. Call your doctor today, or 911.
</div>

## Good evidence

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Honey for a cough with a cold

<p class="dose">Good evidence</p>

**What the research says:** Across studies of upper-respiratory infections, honey eased symptoms, especially how often and how badly people coughed, compared with usual care (E32).

**How Sun makes it:** 1 to 2 teaspoons of honey stirred into warm (not boiling) water or ginger tea, or straight off the spoon, up to a few times a day while you have the cough.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Never give honey to babies under 1 year. Diabetes: honey counts as sugar. A cough with fever over a few days, shortness of breath, chest pain or blood: not for honey, for your doctor.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

In the studies it beat usual care for a cough with a cold. It costs less than most of the cough aisle. Tastier, too.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Two green kiwis a day for constipation

<p class="dose">Good evidence</p>

**What the research says:** In a 4-week study of 75 people with chronic constipation, 2 green kiwis a day improved bowel movements about as much as 100 g of prunes or 12 g of psyllium, with the fewest side effects, the highest satisfaction and less bloating (E25). An exploratory study: good, not huge.

**How Sun makes it:** Two green kiwis a day, peeled, or scoop them with a spoon. Breakfast is easiest (Morning yogurt bowl).

**Who should skip or ask first:** Kiwi allergy (more common in people with latex allergy). Go up slowly and drink water. Blood in the stool, black stool, weight loss you can't explain, or a big change in your bowel habits: doctor, not kiwi.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Put the onion in the soup. Put the kiwi in your mouth.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### The after-dinner walk

<p class="dose">Good evidence</p>

**What the research says:** Light walking after meals, even 2 to 5 minutes, lowers the rise in blood sugar after eating compared with sitting (E23).

**How Sun makes it:** Walk 5 to 15 minutes after your biggest meal. Inside counts: kitchen to front door and back, along the counter.

**Who should skip or ask first:** If you have diabetes, keep taking your medicines exactly as prescribed; this is on top, not instead. Chest pain or unusual breathlessness when you walk: stop and call your doctor.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Not a remedy. A walk. That's why it works.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Fiber, 25 to 29 grams a day

<p class="dose">Good evidence</p>

**What the research says:** In a large Lancet review, people eating 25 to 29 g of fiber a day had 15 to 30% lower rates of death and heart disease and lower rates of type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer than people eating the least (E24). These are links from long-term studies.

**How Sun makes it:** Climb the fiber ladder: kiwi, brown rice, edamame, prunes and flax, oats, vegetables at every meal.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Go up slowly with water. Ask your doctor first if you've had a bowel blockage, have Crohn's disease or a narrowed bowel, trouble swallowing, or were told to eat low-fiber.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Boring. Works. Most things that work are boring.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Salt substitute (potassium salt)

<p class="dose">Good evidence</p>

**What the research says:** In a trial of 20,995 older adults at high risk, those using a salt substitute that was 25% potassium chloride had fewer strokes, fewer major heart events and fewer deaths than those using regular salt (E35).

**How Sun makes it:** Only with your doctor's okay: use the salt substitute in place of regular salt at the table and in cooking.

**Who should skip or ask first:** **Kidney disease, or on blood-pressure pills like ACE inhibitors, or any medicine that raises potassium? Ask your doctor first. This one is not optional.** Too much potassium can be dangerous for those people.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Good evidence. Also the one on this page most likely to hurt the wrong person. Ask first.
</div>

## Some evidence

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Kimchi and other fermented foods

<p class="dose">Some evidence</p>

**What the research says:** In a 10-week study of 36 adults, a diet high in fermented foods (yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, kombucha; about 6 servings a day by the end) increased gut-microbe diversity and lowered 19 inflammation-related proteins in the blood (E26). Small and short: interesting, not proven for health outcomes.

**How Sun makes it:** A small side of kimchi with meals, plain yogurt with breakfast. You don't need six servings to enjoy it.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Kimchi is salty: watching sodium, small portions or rinse it. Very spicy kimchi can bother reflux. Weakened immune system (for example during chemotherapy): ask your care team which fermented foods are okay for you.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

My mother would say it was obvious. Science took until 2021. Fine. Welcome.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Ginger for nausea

<p class="dose">Some evidence</p>

**What the research says:** Ginger for nausea has reasonable support in research reviews. For knee osteoarthritis pain, ginger had only a small effect compared with placebo, with more stomach complaints (E33). So: may help a little.

**How Sun makes it:** Ginger tea: 5 or 6 thin slices of fresh ginger simmered in 2 cups of water for 10 minutes. Add honey if you like.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Food amounts of ginger are fine for most people. Ginger **supplements** (capsules, extracts): on blood thinners? Ask your doctor first. Nausea that won't stop, vomiting blood, or black stool: doctor, today.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Good in tea. Better in bulgogi.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Gargling plain water in cold season

<p class="dose">Some evidence</p>

**What the research says:** In one Japanese trial of 387 healthy adults aged 18 to 65, gargling plain water daily for 60 days was linked with 36% fewer upper-respiratory infections than usual care. There was no fake-gargle comparison, and nobody over 65 was studied (E56).

**How Sun makes it:** A few gargles of plain tap water, after you come home, in cold season.

**Who should skip or ask first:** If you have trouble swallowing or choke easily, skip it. Salt-water gargles for a sore throat are fine for comfort; don't swallow them if you watch your sodium.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

One study. Young people. Cheap. Harmless. I do it. I don't brag about it.
</div>

## Tradition only: enjoy it as food

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Chicken and ginger soup for a cold

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** Chicken soup slowed white blood cells in a lab dish. The researchers themselves said whether it helps people is 'untested' (E57). What's true: when you're sick, warm fluids, salt and protein you can actually swallow help you keep eating and drinking.

**How Sun makes it:** Chicken, ginger and jujube soup, or the rice porridge.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Watch sodium if you're on a salt limit (make it with low-sodium broth). Fever that lasts, shortness of breath, confusion: doctor.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

It won't fix your cold. It will make you feel looked after. That's not nothing.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Barley tea (boricha)

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** No good research on health effects. It's a warm, caffeine-free drink many Korean families drink instead of water.

**How Sun makes it:** 1 Tbsp roasted barley (or a barley tea bag) in 4 cups water, simmer 5 minutes. Hot or cold.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Celiac disease or gluten sensitivity: barley has gluten, skip it.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

It's water that tastes like toast. Drink more water. That's the whole trick.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Jujube (red date) tea

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** No trustworthy human research for the claims you'll read online. Dried jujubes are a sweet fruit.

**How Sun makes it:** 6 dried jujubes, sliced, plus 3 slices of ginger, simmered in 4 cups water for 20 minutes.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Dried fruit is sugar: diabetes, count it. Watch for the pits if you have dentures.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Sweet, warm, lovely at night. Enjoy it. Don't expect it to do your homework.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Seaweed soup (miyeok-guk)

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** Eaten for birthdays and after childbirth in Korea. No good research on it as a remedy. Seaweed does contain a lot of iodine, and the amount varies hugely: commercially sold seaweeds measured 16 to 2,984 micrograms of iodine per gram (E58).

**How Sun makes it:** The seaweed soup recipe in this book.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Thyroid condition (especially autoimmune thyroid disease)? Ask your doctor how much seaweed is okay (E58).

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

I eat it on birthdays. That's the tradition. The birthday is the medicine.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Rice porridge (jook) for an upset stomach

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** No trials. It's easy to swallow, easy to digest, and gets fluid and some protein in when nothing else sounds good.

**How Sun makes it:** The chicken and ginger rice porridge, made thinner with extra broth.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Vomiting that won't stop, signs of dehydration (very little urine, dizziness), blood, or severe belly pain: doctor, today.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

What mothers feed children when they're sick. Also what children should feed mothers.
</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

### Peppermint tea for the stomach

<p class="dose">Tradition only: enjoy it as food</p>

**What the research says:** The research is for enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules, which improved IBS symptoms and belly pain compared with placebo (E34). That's a pharmacy product, not tea. For the tea itself: tradition.

**How Sun makes it:** A mug after dinner if you like it.

**Who should skip or ask first:** Peppermint can make reflux and heartburn worse. Thinking about the capsules? That's a supplement: ask your doctor or pharmacist, especially if you take prescriptions.

</div>

<div class="sun" markdown="1">
<div class="who">Sun Yoon</div>

Nice tea. Not the same as the study. Know the difference.
</div>

## Don't bother

The internet loves these. The evidence doesn't. Each one is marked **Myth** so nobody screenshots it the wrong way.

| Myth | What's actually true |
|---|---|
| ✗ **Myth:** Onion in a glass of water, or onion slices in your socks | No evidence of any benefit to your body (EVIDENCE.md, deliberately-not-claimed list). Put the onion in the soup. |
| ✗ **Myth:** Detox teas and 'cleanses' | No competent evidence that detox products do anything. Your liver and kidneys already do this job, every day, for free. |
| ✗ **Myth:** A drink that 'burns sugar' after dinner | No drink has that evidence. The after-dinner walk does (E23). |
| ✗ **Myth:** Anything that 'lowers blood pressure instantly' | Slow breathing can lower blood pressure for a short time (E19). Resting blood pressure comes down over weeks of training, like wall sits and strength work (E20), plus food and the medicines your doctor manages. Never stop or change blood-pressure medicine on your own. |
| ✗ **Myth:** Salt or bay leaves under your feet, cabbage leaves for any pain | No evidence. For back pain, the thing with the evidence is exercise: 249 trials (E30). |


# How we calculated the numbers

**Source.** Every ingredient is matched to a food in the USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy database (April 2018 release, downloaded from fdc.nal.usda.gov, E52). We took energy (kcal), protein, total dietary fiber and sodium per 100 grams, multiplied by the grams used, added up the recipe and divided by the number of servings.

**Two pastes aren't in the USDA database:** gochujang and chunjang. For those we used the manufacturer label values recorded on Open Food Facts (Sempio gochujang, Obok chunjang, E53). The chunjang label's protein (20 g per 100 g) looks high for a bean paste, so treat the protein in Chang's black bean noodles as a slight overestimate (the paste adds about 3.6 g per serving).

**Rules we followed.**

- Meat, fish and tofu are weighed **raw**, matched to raw USDA values. Rice and pasta are weighed **cooked**, matched to cooked values (1 cup cooked brown rice = 195 g; 1 cup cooked whole-wheat pasta = 140 g).
- Salt, soy sauce and pastes are counted in full at the amounts listed. "Pinch" and "to taste" items, and water, count as zero.
- Dried wakame is calculated as its soaked weight (1/2 oz dry ≈ 140 g soaked) using USDA raw wakame.
- Where USDA reports no value for a nutrient (fiber in raw shrimp and short-grain white rice), we counted zero. Shrimp has essentially no fiber; white rice has a little, so those fiber numbers are slightly low.
- Soy-braised eggs: all the soy sauce is counted even though most stays in the pot, so sodium is overstated.
- Brand, ripeness and exact size change real numbers. Treat these as good estimates, within about 10%.

Numbers are rounded: protein to the nearest gram, fiber to 0.1 g, calories and sodium to the nearest 10.

# Where the numbers come from

Every number and health statement in this book traces to one of the entries below. They are the same evidence IDs our whole team uses (EVIDENCE.md). Grade A means a Cochrane review, a large meta-analysis or a guideline body. B means a single good trial or a small meta-analysis. C means an observational study: it shows a link, not cause and effect. D means lab, physiology or label data.


<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E19** (grade A− (meta)). Voluntary slow breathing (around 6 breaths/min) increases vagally-mediated heart-rate variability during and after practice.

<p class="src">Source: Laborde et al., Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2022 — https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149763422002007</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E20** (grade A). Exercise and resting BP: 270 RCTs, 15,827 people. Isometric training lowered BP the most (−8.24/−4.00 mmHg). Wall squat ranked top for systolic. Aerobic −4.49/−2.53, dynamic resistance −4.55/−3.04. These are average changes over weeks of training, not instant.

<p class="src">Source: Edwards et al., BJSM 2023 — https://bmjgroup.com/static-isometric-exercise-such-as-wall-sits-best-for-lowering-blood-pressure/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E23** (grade A− (meta)). Light walking after meals (even 2–5 minutes) lowers the post-meal glucose rise compared with sitting.

<p class="src">Source: Buffey et al., Sports Med 2022 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35147898/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E24** (grade A (meta of cohorts + RCTs)). Fiber: 25–29 g/day was linked with 15–30% lower all-cause and CV mortality, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer. More fiber was linked with more benefit.

<p class="src">Source: Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019 — https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)31809-9/fulltext</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E25** (grade B (exploratory)). Chronic constipation: 2 green kiwifruit/day vs 100 g prunes vs 12 g psyllium, 4 weeks, 75 patients. All three improved bowel movements similarly. Kiwi had the fewest side effects and highest satisfaction, and improved bloating.

<p class="src">Source: Chey et al., Am J Gastroenterol 2021 — https://www.healio.com/news/gastroenterology/20210608/kiwi-fruit-effectively-relieves-symptoms-in-chronic-constipation</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E26** (grade B (small)). 36 adults, 10 weeks. A high-fermented-food diet (yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut, kombucha; intake rose to about 6 servings/day by the end) increased microbiome diversity and lowered 19 inflammatory proteins (including IL-6). The high-fiber arm didn't show those changes over 10 weeks.

<p class="src">Source: Wastyk et al., Cell 2021 — https://med.stanford.edu/news/all-news/2021/07/fermented-food-diet-increases-microbiome-diversity-lowers-inflammation.html</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E27** (grade B). Prune Study: postmenopausal women eating 50 g prunes/day (about 5–6) preserved total hip BMD over 12 months vs controls.

<p class="src">Source: De Souza et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2022 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9193411/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E28** (grade A (consensus)). PROT-AGE: adults over 65 should get 1.0–1.2 g protein/kg/day, and 1.2–1.5 g/kg if active or ill (unless there is severe kidney disease). Aim for 25–30 g per meal with about 2.5–2.8 g leucine.

<p class="src">Source: Bauer et al., JAMDA 2013 — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23867520/</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E30** (grade A). Exercise for chronic low back pain: 249 trials, 24,486 people. Pain about 15 points better (0–100 scale) at 3 months vs no treatment or usual care. Function improved modestly.

<p class="src">Source: Hayden et al., Cochrane 2021 — https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD009790_exercise-treatment-chronic-low-back-pain</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E32** (grade A−). Honey improved upper-respiratory-infection symptoms, especially cough frequency and severity, compared with usual care. Never give honey to infants under 12 months.

<p class="src">Source: Abuelgasim et al., BMJ Evid Based Med 2021 — https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/news/honey-better-than-usual-care-for-easing-respiratory-symptoms-especially-cough</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E33** (grade A−). Ginger for osteoarthritis pain: small effect vs placebo, with more GI complaints. Say it "may help a little". Ginger for nausea has reasonable support. It can interact with blood thinners at supplement doses.

<p class="src">Source: Bartels et al., Osteoarthritis Cartilage 2015 — https://www.oarsijournal.com/article/S1063-4584(14)00641-4/fulltext ; ginger umbrella review AJCN 2022 — https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(22)00277-5/fulltext</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E34** (grade A−). Enteric-coated peppermint oil improved global IBS symptoms and abdominal pain vs placebo. It can worsen reflux.

<p class="src">Source: Alammar et al., BMC Complement Altern Med 2019 — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12906-018-2409-0</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E35** (grade B+). Salt substitute (25% potassium chloride) in 20,995 older adults at high risk: stroke, major CV events and death were all reduced. Caution: potassium salt isn't for people with kidney disease or on potassium-raising medicines. Always say "ask your doctor first".

<p class="src">Source: Neal et al., NEJM 2021 (SSaSS) — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2105675</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E52** (grade A (reference database)). USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy (April 2018 release): per-100 g energy, protein, total dietary fiber, sodium and leucine used for every recipe calculation in Sun Yoon's Strong Kitchen (FDC IDs listed per ingredient in the book's method appendix).

<p class="src">Source: Opened/downloaded https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-datasets/FoodData_Central_sr_legacy_food_csv_2018-04.zip</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E53** (grade D (label data)). Label values for two Korean pastes not in SR Legacy, per 100 g: Sempio gochujang (barcode 8801005000178) 233 kcal, 5.0 g protein, 2.7 g fiber, 2,640 mg sodium; Obok chunjang (8801126032447) 200 kcal, 20 g protein, 0 g fiber, 3,200 mg sodium (single crowd-sourced label; protein looks high, so treat as approximate).

<p class="src">Source: Open Food Facts API — opened https://world.openfoodfacts.org/product/8801005000178 , https://world.openfoodfacts.org/product/8801126032447</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E54** (grade A (federal guidance)). Safe minimum internal temperatures: ground meat 160°F; beef/pork steaks, chops, roasts 145°F + 3-minute rest; all poultry 165°F; fish 145°F or until opaque and flaking; shrimp until pearly/opaque; clams until shells open; eggs until yolk and white are firm; egg dishes 160°F; leftovers 165°F.

<p class="src">Source: FoodSafety.gov — opened https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E55** (grade A (federal guidance)). Adults 65+ are at higher risk of foodborne illness (weaker immune response, slower gut transit, less stomach acid, reduced liver and kidney clearance).

<p class="src">Source: FoodSafety.gov — opened https://www.foodsafety.gov/people-at-risk/older-adults</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E56** (grade B− (single RCT, unblinded)). Water gargling RCT (Japan): 387 healthy volunteers aged 18–65, 60 days. Gargling plain water daily was linked with 36% fewer upper-respiratory infections vs usual care; povidone-iodine gargle showed no significant difference. No sham/placebo arm (critics note possible bias). Not studied in adults over 65.

<p class="src">Source: Satomura et al., Am J Prev Med 2005 (primary abstract page returned 403: primary not opened, unverified). Opened secondary report: https://www.infectioncontroltoday.com/view/gargling-may-prevent-colds-expert-finds-results-hard-swallow</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E57** (grade D (in vitro)). Chicken soup slowed white-blood-cell (neutrophil) movement in a lab dish. The authors state clinical benefit "remains untested". Lab evidence only: tradition, enjoy it as food.

<p class="src">Source: Rennard et al., Chest 2000 — opened https://www.unmc.edu/strategic-communications/for-the-media/press-kits/files/chickensouppublishedstudy2000.pdf</p>

</div>

<div class="keep" markdown="1">

**E58** (grade A (NIH fact sheet)). Seaweed iodine varies enormously: commercially available seaweeds measured 16 to 2,984 mcg iodine per gram. Adult upper limit 1,100 mcg/day from all sources. People with autoimmune thyroid disease may have adverse effects at intakes considered safe for others.

<p class="src">Source: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — opened https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iodine-HealthProfessional/ , https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Iodine-Consumer/</p>

</div>
